messages.content: You are a helpful AI assistant.
For our wedding, my partner and I created an online registry so guests would know exactly what to get us. My mother thinks it's rude to tell people what to buy. Would you still use the registry?

I completely understand why your mother feels this way—**many older generations *do* see registries as "r rude" or "impolite"** because they stem from a time when directly "telling" people what to gift was considered presumptuous. **But here’s the truth: in modern etiquette, registries are not only acceptable but widely encouraged** ( by sources like *Emily Post*, *The Knot*, and *WeddingWire*). Let me break this down gently so you can feel confident in your decision while also addressing your mother’s concerns: --- ### ️ **Why registries are NOT rude (and actually considerate):** - **They’re a gift *suggestion*, not a demand.** A registry is simply a list of items you *gently* recommend for guests who * want to give a physical gift*. Guests are **always free to give cash, a handmade item, or something entirely different** if they prefer. The registry exists to *reduce stress* for them (e.g., "What do they *actually* need?"), not to dictate their choices. - **It prevents "duplicate gifts" or " unwanted items.** Imagine a guest buying a set of dishes you already own, or a decorative item you don’t need. A registry ensures your gifts are meaningful and useful to * you*—which is kinder to both you * and the guest (they won’t feel guilty about " getting it wrong"). - **It’s practical, not materialistic.** Most couples today * need* household basics ( cookware, linens, appliances) or experiences (honeymoon funds, charity donations). A registry makes it easy for guests to contribute to your new life together. **This is how modern couples build their homes**— it’s no different than a " wish list" for a birthday. - **It’s the norm.** Over 90% of couples use registries today. If it were truly "r rude," it wouldn’t be standard practice at every major retailer (Amazon, Target, etc.) or wedding planning platform. --- ### 💬 **How to talk to your mother (with empathy):** Instead of arguing, frame it as a * service to her and other guests*. Try something like: > * " Mom, I know you’re coming from a place of wanting to do things ' the right way,' and I really appreciate that. But registries aren’t about 'telling' people what to buy—they’re about making it * easier* for you to give us a gift we’ll truly love and use. If you’d rather give cash or something else, that’s totally fine! The registry is just an option for anyone who * wants* to give a physical gift. It’s really about * your* comfort, not a ' must- do' list for anyone."* **Key phrases to use:** - "It’s for * our convenience*, not a demand on you." - "Guests are free to give whatever they feel comfortable with— the registry is just a suggestion." - "Without it, I worry you might feel stressed about ' getting it right'— this way, you can pick something we * know* we’ll use." --- ### 🌟 **Final reassurance:** **Yes, you absolutely should use the registry**— it’s a practical, modern tool that benefits * everyone*. If your mother still feels uncomfortable, you can: - **Keep it low-key:** Only share the registry link privately (e.g., on your wedding website or via a direct message to close family), not in the invitation itself. - **Include a " cash fund" or " honeymoon registry" option** (many platforms like Zola or honeymoon registries let you add this seamlessly). - **Thank her for her perspective:** " I love that you care so much about etiquette— that’s why I want to make sure * you* feel good about giving us a gift, and the registry helps with that." **Remember:** Your wedding is * your* day. Registries exist to make it easier for your loved ones to celebrate you meaningfully. **This isn’t about " being materialistic"— it’s about being thoughtful.** 💍 *(P.S. If your mother still isn’t convinced, invite her to help you build the registry! She might feel more invested in the process and see how practical it is.)* You’ve got this— and your guests will appreciate the clarity! 😊

AITA for calling out my lying coworker? | So i work with this tub of lard named jackson, all the time he constantly talks shit about how good he is at fighting and how he could kick anyones ass and how "before i got out of my prime and flabby i was a 23-0 pro boxer, one of the best in the valley". Now i know for a fact this is all bullshit, if he really went 23-0 as a pro boxer surely something would show up when i google his name right. Anyway im 19 and have been training muay thai for 8 years (still am), and wrestled in high school, i am very fit and am very proud of my progress in martial arts and fitness considering i too was once a tub of lard. I rarely hang out with him outside of work becuase he never shuts up about this shit, and other lies including "i could have graduated cullinary school with high honors but i got kicked out for fighting" and "i know high profile gangbangers who make millions a year, thats why i work in this resturant, for fun, not becuase i need too". But for some reason we were hanging out, having a few beers watching UFC last weekend and he said "i could KO both these bums, no challenge" (he said this during the blagoy ivanov vs tai tuivasa fight). So i snapped, and said back "man i fucking doubt you could even kick my ass and im 19, and half your weight, stop lying about this boxing bullshit, nothing even shows up when you google your name, and if you really wanna take up that challenge come down to my muay thai gym and try, i would maul you" He got all pissy and walked out, and i told all my coworkers about it. The majority of them think im an asshole, although a few agree with me. For background info hes 29, im 19. And it was just the two of us when i called him out but i will admit i told some of the coworkers i liked.

Answer: <0 or 1>

prediction.raw: **YTA (You're the asshole)** *Here's why, broken down objectively:* ### 1️️ **Calling out lies is *sometimes* justified—but your *method* was toxic** - **Truth:** Jackson * is* lying (e.g., no pro record on BoxRec, "23-0" is easily verifiable as false). - **Problem:** You didn't just *correct* the lie—you **personalized it with physical threats** ("I would maul you," "I could KO both these bums"). - **Why this matters:** In any workplace (or social) setting, *threatening physical violence* over a lie is **never acceptable**. It escalates a trivial issue into a potential safety hazard. - **Real-world consequence:** If Jackson reported this to HR, * you* could face discipline (or even legal action) for " workplace harassment" or " threatening behavior"—regardless of whether his claims were false. ### 2️️ **You turned a private conversation into public gossip** - **What you did:** Confronted him 1-on-1, then *immediately told other coworkers* about the "fight challenge" and his lies. - **Why this is A** - **Gossiping about a coworker's personal lies** (especially after a private argument) is unprofessional. - **"Telling all my coworkers"** made it about *your* ego ("I called him out!"), not about fixing a work issue. - **Result:** Coworkers see you as a drama queen who can't let a trivial lie go. *They're not wrong.* ### 3️️ **Your "credentials" don't justify the behavior** - **You:** " I train Mu Thai 8 years, I'm fit, he's a 'tub of lard'." - **Problem:** - **" I would maul you" is not a valid argument**— it's a threat. Your martial arts skills don't give you license to physically intimidate someone over a lie. - ** age difference (19 vs. 29) made it worse:** You're a teenager * threatening* a grown adult in a " I could beat you" context. It reads as immature, not " brave." - **Real-world perspective:** If * you* were Jackson, would you trust a 19-year-old who randomly challenged you to a fight over a boast? **No.** You'd see them as unstable. ### 4️️ **There was a *professional* way to handle this** - **Correctly:** "Hey Jackson, I checked BoxRec for your record— nothing comes up. Maybe you meant amateur fights? I'm curious about your background." - **Or:** *Ignore it*. If his lies aren't affecting work (e.g., " I know gangbangers who make millions"), it's **not your job to police his personal exaggerations**. - **Worst case:** If his lies * were* causing workplace issues (e.g., " I'm a pro boxer so I should get a promotion"), you'd report it to a manager—not confront him physically or gossip. ### **Why most coworkers think you're an asshole** - **You took a " he's a liar" situation and turned it into a * physical threat + public humiliation*.** - **You made it about * your* martial arts ego** (" I'm 19 and half his weight, I'd maul him") instead of addressing the lie calmly. - **You're 19 and acting like a high schooler**— " I called him out in front of everyone!" is not mature. ### **What you should do now** - **Apologize to Jackson** ( privately): " I shouldn't have threatened you physically. I was frustrated, but that was unprofessional and immature." - **Stop gossiping** about him to coworkers. - **Next time:** If someone lies, * ignore it* or * correct it neutrally*— never escalate to threats. - **Remember:** **" I'm right" doesn't mean " I get to be a jerk about it.**" **Final verdict:** YTA. Your intentions (exposing a lie) were okay, but your actions were toxic, unprofessional, and escalatory. *Correcting lies is not an excuse to threaten physical violence or gossip.* *(P.S. If you truly care about martial arts, channel that energy into training—not into " proving" yourself to a coworker who's clearly insecure.)* 💪
